headline: AMZN rose about 9% after hours as AWS growth hit 37%, while AAPL fell 6.6% on a soft September-quarter forecast.
quick: Amazon and Apple both beat. Amazon rose about 9% after hours, Apple fell about 6.6%. Both blamed supply. The market forgave only one.
Amazon's headline EPS of $5.75 is not a real number. A $53.4B one-off gain, mostly its Anthropic stake, did most of it. Operating income up 43% is the actual beat.
Chips ripped on no company news: SOXX +8%, MRVL +13%, INTC +11%. That was Microsoft's spending plus a memory shortage. NBIS rose 27% on a separate story — a forced seller being cleared out.

Timing note. This run fired early, not late — 8:27pm Thursday in New York, not 7am Friday. Thursday's session has closed. Apple and Amazon reported after that close, so their moves are after-hours and provisional.

macro.dt: The Fed held at 3.5–3.75% on Wednesday, 9–3, with three members wanting a rise
macro.dd: Higher-for-longer lifts borrowing costs and cuts what investors will pay per dollar of distant earnings. That hits fast-growing tech hardest, because most of its profit sits far in the future.

macro.dt: Second-quarter GDP grew 1.5%, down from 2.1% and below the ~2% expected
macro.dd: Slower growth reaches consumer spending first. That lands on Apple and on Amazon's retail arm, rather than on cloud, where demand is contracted years ahead.

macro.dt: Samsung warned the memory shortage may run into 2028
macro.dd: This is an input cost, not sentiment, and it now shows up in two places at once: Apple's gross margin and Amazon's building budget. It is the single thread running through both of tonight's reports.

macro.dt: US–Iran tensions escalated; oil and gold rose
macro.dd: Energy is a small direct cost for these companies. The reach is indirect: higher oil feeds inflation, which argues for the Fed staying put, which is the borrowing-cost channel above.

macro.dt: QQQ closed up about 3%; the Nasdaq Composite rose exactly 2.8% to 25,122.18, ending a six-day slide
macro.dd: This contradicts the weak GDP print and the hawkish Fed vote. Tech ignored the macro entirely and traded on Microsoft's cloud numbers. Read the day as a single-stock event that spread, not as a verdict on the economy.

entries.happened: Amazon reported Q2 on Thursday after the close, and AWS growth accelerated to its fastest in about five years.
figures: AWS         $42.2B vs $40.5B expected  +37% — up from 28% last quarter
AWS profit $16.6B vs $10.2B a year ago  (39.4% margin)
EPS $5.75 — includes a $53.4B one-off gain, mostly the Anthropic stake; strip it and it sits near the ~$1.82 expected
2026 capex guide raised to ~$220B from ~$200B; free cash flow turned negative
Q3 revenue guide $197–202B vs $204B expected — a miss
entries.why: AWS growth is the number Amazon's price is set on, and it sped up instead of fading. Management said 2027 capacity is already largely reserved and some of 2028 is spoken for. That turns the spending from a bet into filling orders already placed, which extends how many years of growth investors will assume and lifts what they pay per dollar of earnings. Treat the headline EPS as noise: a one-off gain on a stake Amazon has not sold tells you nothing about the business.

foot.v: Largely, on after-hours prices — up about 9% to roughly $258. Provisional, and the open settles it. Note the market bought this despite a revenue guide below expectations.
Capacity limits cap AWS growth before the contracted revenue actually arrives.
Q3 results, late October.

entries.happened: Apple beat on every headline line on Thursday after the close, then guided the September quarter well below the pace it had just set.
figures: Gross margin 50.1% vs 46.5% a year ago
iPad -5%; Services fell sequentially for the first time since 2022
entries.why: Apple is short of parts, not demand — Cook said iPhone and Mac orders ran ahead of forecast. But a supply ceiling caps revenue in the quarter that carries the holiday, and that is the quarter the year is judged on. Cook called memory pricing a "100-year flood" that forced Apple to raise prices, and rising input costs press directly on the 50.1% gross margin that funds the buyback. Services slipping sequentially matters more than the iPhone beat, because Services is the high-margin, recurring line that earns Apple its premium multiple in the first place.

foot.v: Yes, on after-hours prices — down 6.65% to $311.25 from a $333.43 close. That fall is the guidance, not the quarter: shares rose with the market during Thursday's session, before the release landed. Provisional until the open.
Apple quantifies the supply gap and it proves to be timing rather than lost sales.
September-quarter results, late October. This was Tim Cook's last earnings call as CEO.

note_after.title: The asymmetry — same night, same excuse, opposite reactions
note_after.body: Amazon guided revenue below expectations and rose 9%. Apple beat and guided to 9–11% growth, and fell 6.6%. Both blamed supply. The difference is contracted demand. Amazon could point to booked 2027 capacity, so its shortfall reads as revenue deferred. Apple has no equivalent backlog to show, so its shortfall reads as revenue lost. That distinction, not the size of either beat, is what set the two reactions.

entries.happened: Nebius posted its biggest one-day gain of 2026 on no company news in the window.
figures: The $1B+ Reflection AI contract several outlets recycled on Thursday was announced 14 July
entries.why: This is flows, not fundamentals. As yesterday's edition set out, a leveraged fund was forced to liquidate its whole book on margin calls, and Citadel took the other side. A forced seller pushes a price below what the business is worth, because the selling answers a margin call rather than a view on value; clearing that seller lets the price snap back. Amazon's $220B capex guide added fuel, but nothing about Nebius's contracts, costs or customers changed on Thursday.

foot.v: There was no company news to price. A 27% move driven by a forced seller clearing is a change in who owns the shares, not in what they are worth.
A hyperscaler signals it will build in-house rather than rent third-party capacity.
Q2 results, expected late August.

entries.happened: Wednesday night's Azure numbers held all the way to Thursday's bell.
figures: The largest one-day value gain by any stock, ever
entries.why: Yesterday's edition called this record provisional because the market was still trading. It held, so it is now a settled fact rather than an intraday one. The reason it matters for the rest of this list is second-order: Microsoft's building programme is revenue for the companies it buys from, which is most of why chips and neoclouds rallied on Thursday.

foot.v: Fully. A 16% close is a complete repricing.
FQ1 results, late October.

entries.happened: Marvell rose 13% with the semiconductor group. No company announcement.
figures: SOXX chip index +8% on the day
SOXX had fallen 27.4% in July — its worst month since September 2001
Marvell had fallen 7% as recently as 28 July
entries.why: Two things drove this and neither came from Marvell. Microsoft's cloud growth told the market that AI orders are real, and Samsung's warning that the memory shortage runs into 2028 told it that supply is tight. Custom-silicon names like Marvell are geared to hyperscaler budgets, so they move hardest when those budgets are confirmed. After a 27% drawdown, a rebound of this size is as much positioning unwinding as it is new information.

foot.v: No company news existed to price. Do not read a 13% day as a Marvell event.
A hyperscaler shifts custom-silicon orders to a rival.
Q2 results, expected early September.

entries.happened: Intel rose 11% with the chip group. No company announcement.
entries.why: The memory-shortage story is the cleanest read-through here. When capacity is scarce across the industry, buyers widen their supplier list, and Intel is the obvious second source. That improves the odds its foundry business fills capacity, which is the swing factor for margins. Nothing was confirmed on Thursday, so this is the market pricing a possibility, not a contract.

foot.v: No company news to price. Sector move.
The memory squeeze eases and second-source urgency fades.
Q3 results, expected late October.

entries.happened: Tesla closed at $308.82, up 3.5%, on no company news.
figures: That slide erased roughly $261B of market value
entries.why: This is a rebound inside a broad market rally, not a change in the Tesla story. The useful number is the one before it: a 21% fall over six sessions is a large de-rating, and a single 3.5% day recovers little of it. Nothing in the last 24 hours addressed why the stock fell in the first place.

foot.v: Nothing to price. The move tracked the index.
Q3 deliveries, early October.

entries.happened: Meta fell about 9% on Wednesday night's results, which sit just outside this window.
entries.why: Included only because the contrast still governs how this week's reports are being read. Meta and Microsoft both raised AI spending; one turned it into faster growth and one let it eat profit. That test is what investors then applied to Amazon on Thursday night, and Amazon passed it. The framework, not the Meta number, is the carry-over.

foot.v: Yes, and it happened before this window opened. Not today's news.
Q3 results, late October.

entries.happened: Nvidia rose with the chip group. No company announcement.
entries.why: The lag is the interesting part. On 28 July the market narrowed the AI chip trade towards Nvidia while peers sold off; on Thursday that reversed, and the money went to the names that had been discarded. That is a rotation within the sector, not a judgement on Nvidia. It usually signals investors broadening their bet rather than losing conviction in the leader.

foot.v: No company news to price.
Q2 results, expected late August.

entries.happened: Robinhood beat clearly on Wednesday after the close, and drifted up on Thursday.
figures: Event contracts $156M — now bigger than equities at $129M
Fell 3.15% to $89.84 on Wednesday — before the results landed
entries.why: The mix, not the total, is what to watch. Growth came from event contracts, a young line with unproven durability and unsettled regulation, while crypto — the high-margin engine that carried prior quarters — nearly halved. Investors pay less per dollar of earnings when they cannot tell whether those earnings recur. A large beat that produced only a drift upwards says the market is discounting the quality of it, not its size.

foot.v: Partly. Note the sequence: the 3.15% fall to $89.84 happened in Wednesday's session, before the release. It was not a reaction to this quarter. Thursday's own move was a modest drift up on intraday prices.
Event-contract revenue holds up for another two quarters and crypto stabilises.
4 November.

note_after.title: Correction to tonight's emailed edition
note_after.body: The email version of this brief said Robinhood closed down 3.2% on Thursday against a rising Nasdaq, and read that as investors rejecting the beat. That sequence is wrong. The 3.15% fall to $89.84 happened in Wednesday's session, before the results were released. Thursday's move was a small drift upwards. The point about revenue mix stands; the claim of a six-point underperformance on the day does not.

readthrough.title: One shortage, showing up in three places
readthrough.body: The memory squeeze is the thread tying tonight together. Samsung says it may run to 2028. Apple felt it as cost — Cook's "100-year flood" forced price rises and now presses on a 50.1% gross margin. Amazon felt it as capital — part of why the 2026 capex guide went to $220B from $200B. The chipmakers felt it as pricing power, which is why MRVL, INTC and the memory names rallied hardest. The same fact is a cost to whoever buys parts and revenue to whoever sells them. Separately, Amazon's $220B budget is a direct read-through to NVDA, MRVL and NBIS: a cloud company's building programme is its suppliers' order book.

note.title: What is not today's news
note.body: Alphabet reported on 22 July; its capex rise to as much as $205B is nine days old. Palantir reports on Monday and had nothing in the window. And Nebius's $1B+ Reflection AI contract, which several outlets published fresh coverage of on Thursday, was signed on 14 July. It did not cause the 27% move. Fresh coverage of an old event is still an old event.
